pedagogy.summary: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator: 0.375 = 375/1000, which simplifies to 3/8. Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to 10, 100, 1000… Whether a fraction terminates is decided entirely by the prime factors of its denominator in lowest terms: only 2 and 5 (the prime factors of ten) give a terminating decimal; any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) produces a recurring decimal. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three notations for one value.
bestPractices: Read a decimal by its LAST place value to get the denominator (0.375 = 375 thousandths), then simplify to lowest terms
Teach fraction→decimal two ways — as division (numerator ÷ denominator) AND as scaling the denominator to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125)
Make the '2s and 5s only' test explicit by contrasting terminators (1/8, 1/20, 1/40) with recurrers (1/3, 1/6, 1/7) and factorising each denominator
Treat FDP as three views of one number on a triple number line so conversion is re-notation, not new arithmetic
Show a recurring decimal actually recurring (1/3 = 0.333…) so children do not truncate it and call it exact
keyRepresentations: FDP triple number line / equivalence cards
commonMisconceptions: Reads 0.375 as 375/100 (denominator doesn't match the last place value)
Inverts the division, computing 8 ÷ 3 instead of 3 ÷ 8
Believes every fraction terminates, or truncates a recurring decimal (1/3 = 0.3) and treats it as exact
Decides whether a decimal terminates from the numerator or 'how neat it looks' rather than the denominator's prime factors

learn.summary: Terminating decimals and fractions are two notations for one value, with percentages a third. A terminating decimal is read by its LAST place value to get a power-of-ten denominator (0.375 = 375/1000), then simplified (= 3/8). Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125). The deep idea: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (the primes of ten); any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) makes it recur. Learners should both convert fluently in both directions AND predict termination from the denominator's prime factorisation, not by dividing and guessing.

activities.title: Scale to a power of ten — does it land?
feedback: If a learner says 1/6 stops: factorise 6 = 2×3. The factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so no power of ten is a multiple of 6 and the decimal recurs (0.1666…). Show it recurring rather than truncating to 0.17.

If they truncate a recurring decimal and call it exact (1/3 = 0.3): run the division further so the 3s keep coming; 0.333… is not equal to 0.3. (Year 6 learners meet rounding recurring decimals to three decimal places — rounding is an approximation, not the exact value.)

If they decide termination from the numerator or 'how neat it looks': remind them the numerator is irrelevant once the fraction is simplified — only the lowest-terms denominator's prime factors decide.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a fraction that scales onto a power of ten against one that never does, with prime-factor readouts shown together, is intended to make the 2-and-5 rule discoverable rather than merely asserted; sorting fractions and factorising each denominator is a documented route to the rule.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Take 1/8 and try to turn it into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths: find the multiplier (×125) that makes the denominator 1000, giving 125/1000 = 0.125; confirm it 'lands' exactly.
Now try 1/3 the same way: aim for 10, 100, 1000… and find that no power of ten works; carry out the division 1 ÷ 3 and watch the 3s continue (0.333…), a recurring decimal that never stops.
Write each denominator as a product of primes side by side: 8 = 2×2×2; 6 = 2×3; 3 = 3. Mark which denominators are built only from 2s and 5s.
State the rule you discover in your own words, then test it on 1/20, 1/40 (should terminate) and 1/6, 1/7 (should recur), factorising each denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator is built only from the primes 2 and/or 5 — because those are the primes of ten, so the denominator can be scaled to a power of ten. Any other prime factor forces a recurring decimal.

activities.title: Read a decimal by its last place value
feedback: If a learner writes 0.375 = 375/100: the last digit (5) sits in the thousandths place, so the denominator is 1000, not 100. Re-read several decimals aloud by their final place value before writing the fraction.

If they invert the division and compute 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8 (getting 2.66…): re-establish that a/b means a ÷ b — numerator divided by denominator — grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8 people, which gives less than one each (0.375).
activities.rationale: Anchoring the denominator to the last place value is intended to address the most common conversion error (reading onto the wrong power of ten), and practising division-as-conversion in the reverse direction aims to reinforce fraction-as-division, a documented sticking point.
sourceClaims: Converting a fraction to a decimal is the division numerator / denominator (fraction-as-division); understanding fractions as division underpins decimal equivalence and is a documented sticking point.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Name the place value of the LAST digit of 0.375 (thousandths), so the starting denominator is 1000: write 0.375 = 375/1000.
Simplify stepwise to lowest terms: 375/1000 = 3/8 (divide both by 125). Check the simplified fraction against the original decimal.
Repeat with other decimals (0.2 = 2/10 = 1/5; 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4; 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20), each time naming the last place value first.
Reverse the direction: convert 3/8 to a decimal two ways — divide 3 ÷ 8, and scale 3/8 to 375/1000 — and confirm both give 0.375.
activities.intendedInsight: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator; reading the last place value gives that denominator, and simplifying gives lowest terms. Fraction→decimal is division (numerator ÷ denominator), equivalently scaling to a power of ten.

activities.title: Sort, match and fill the gaps (consolidation)
feedback: If a learner sorts by dividing and rounding: that only shows what happens to begin with, not whether it stops forever. Ask them to factorise the denominator in lowest terms and apply the 2-and-5 test instead.
If a chain step is wrong, point back to the place-value reading (last digit → denominator) and the simplification factor (×125 or ÷125).
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and fill-in-and-explain tasks give repeated, checkable practice across both directions and foreground the structural (prime-factor) test over empirical division; the fill-in step asks the learner to produce values and explain each one, so this activity consolidates and partly requires articulation of the discovered rule, not its first teaching.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.
learnerActions: Match terminating decimals to their simplest fractions: 0.375 ↔ 3/8, 0.2 ↔ 1/5, 0.25 ↔ 1/4.
Sort a set of fractions into two columns, 'terminates' and 'recurs', by inspecting each denominator's prime factors (not by dividing): e.g. 7/40 and 1/20 terminate; 5/12 and 1/6 recur.
Fill in the chain 0.375 = __/1000 = __/8, then explain each step (last place value → denominator, then the ÷125 simplification).

Transfer to unfamiliar fractions: predict whether 9/25, 4/15 and 6/15 terminate, justify from the prime factors of each denominator in lowest terms (6/15 = 2/5), then check by converting (9/25 = 0.36; 4/15 = 0.2666…; 6/15 = 0.4).
activities.intendedInsight: Bidirectional conversion to simplest form becomes fluent, and the terminate/recur judgement is made from the denominator's prime factors rather than by trial division.

activities.title: Predict and justify: will it stop? (optional discussion)
feedback: Accept only reasons that cite the denominator's prime factors; 'it looks neat' or 'I tried dividing' is not a structural justification.
If the learner can convert but cannot say why 1/8 stops and 1/6 does not, return to factorising the two denominators side by side.
activities.rationale: A short predict-and-justify exchange is proposed to supplement procedural practice by targeting the 'why do some fractions never stop?' reasoning; it supplements rather than replaces conversion practice, since the objective is procedural fluency. Its effect on reasoning is untested here.
learnerActions: Before converting, predict aloud whether a given fraction (e.g. 1/6, 7/40, 5/12) terminates or recurs, and say WHY from the denominator.
Justify the prediction by naming the prime factors of the denominator and relating them to the primes of ten (2 and 5).
Have a partner or adult pose the question 'How could you know without doing the whole division?' and respond with a reasoned argument, then check by converting.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the prediction and its reason is intended to reveal whether the learner reasons from structure (prime factors) or merely from procedures; articulating the reason aims to strengthen the conceptual link, though that effect is not established here.

constraints: Recurring decimals must be shown genuinely recurring (1/3 = 0.333…); do not truncate (0.3 or 0.33) and call it exact. Rounding a recurring decimal to a set number of places is an approximation introduced for Year 6, not the exact value.
The 2-and-5 rule applies only to the denominator IN LOWEST TERMS; simplify first and ignore the numerator when judging termination.

Matching is recognition-and-recall practice, a sort checks classification of denominators, and a fill-in chain asks the learner to produce values; on their own these task types do not require the learner to carry out a full conversion in both directions and articulate the reason, so pair them with at least one activity where the learner constructs and explains a full conversion and a termination prediction (as the fill-in-and-explain and predict-and-justify steps do).

A tap-to-reveal equivalence card (fraction → decimal → percentage with denominator prime factors) is a useful reference aid but cannot let a learner test the terminate/recur boundary themselves; use it alongside, not instead of, the scaling/conversion work.
Fraction-as-division must be the direction numerator ÷ denominator (3 ÷ 8), not denominator ÷ numerator.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing is made.

Legacy design described two linked on-screen panels (scale-to-power-of-ten with a prime-factor readout, and place-value decimal-to-fraction simplifier) with a 'lights up/it fits' response. These interaction examples are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. A fixed printed chart can still teach the conversions even though it cannot be manipulated.

The legacy source framed interactive scaling as the way the rule 'clicks' and rated dialogue/3D as weaker. Those comparative fit judgements are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the alternatives are kept here as activities with stated purposes and limits rather than as a ranking.

Editorial change: efficacy-asserting wording in the activity rationales and in activity[3]'s intendedInsight ('removes the error', 'reinforces', 'strengthening the conceptual link') was softened to intended/aims wording, since the sources identify the misconceptions/sticking points but do not establish that these specific activities fix them.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (÷125) is correct; 3/8 = 0.375 is correct; 1/8 = 0.125 via ×125 to 125/1000 is correct; 8 = 2³, 6 = 2×3, 3 = 3 are correct; 1/6 = 0.1666… recurs (3 is not 2 or 5) is correct; 7/40 terminates (40 = 2³×5) and 5/12 recurs (12 = 2²×3) are correct; 0.2=1/5, 0.25=1/4, 0.35=7/20 are correct; 8 ÷ 3 = 2.66… correctly identifies the inverted-division error. No arithmetic errors found in learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: What place value is the last digit of 0.375 in? So what denominator do you start with before simplifying?
For 3/8, which number do you divide by which — and why that way round?
Will 1/6 stop or go on forever? What is it about the 6 that tells you, without dividing all the way?
1/8 stops but 1/3 does not. What is different about the denominators when you break each into prime factors?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (dividing by 125); 3/8 = 0.375 (3 ÷ 8, or ×125 to make 375/1000). 1/6 does NOT stop — 6 = 2×3, and the factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so it recurs (0.1666…).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal onto the wrong power of ten: 0.375 = 375/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the last digit's place (thousandths), so the denominator is 1000; then simplify. Re-read several decimals by their final place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denominator does not match the last digit's place value; the simplified fraction is wrong or won't simplify to 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the division for fraction→decimal: computes 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish fraction-as-division: a/b means a ÷ b (numerator into denominator), grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Divides the larger number by the smaller, or gets 2.66… for 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges whether a fraction terminates from the numerator or how 'neat' it looks, or believes every fraction terminates — so claims 1/6 stops, or truncates it to 0.17 and calls it exact
errorPatterns.nextMove: Factorise the denominators side by side (8 = 2³ terminates; 6 = 2×3 recurs) and connect 2 and 5 to the primes of ten; show 1/6 genuinely recurring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 1/6 stops; decides by trying to divide and rounding rather than by the denominator's prime factors; cannot explain WHY 1/8 stops but 1/6 does not

responseLevels.gap: Mis-reads the decimal's denominator or inverts the division; believes all fractions terminate; cannot connect terminating to the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently to simplest form AND predicts termination from the denominator's prime factorisation (only 2 and 5), explaining why (it can be scaled to a power of ten); transfers to a new fraction such as 7/40 (terminates) or 5/12 (recurs).
responseLevels.partial: Converts 0.375 ↔ 3/8 correctly by procedure, but decides termination empirically by dividing and rounding rather than from the denominator's prime factors, or states the 2-and-5 rule only after prompting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 0.375 to a fraction in its simplest form, and convert 3/8 to a decimal. Then tell me — will 1/6 give a decimal that stops, or one that goes on forever? How could you know without doing the whole division?' Watch how they work and listen to the reason for 1/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Converting 0.375 both ways is routine and does not separate understanding from memorised steps. The 1/6 question is the hinge: a child who grasps the structure inspects the denominator's prime factors (only 2 and 5 terminate) and answers WITHOUT dividing; a child who has only procedures tries to divide and rounds, guesses, or asserts that all fractions stop. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly give visibly different responses here.
